To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) AT is a dynamic organ, which adapts to the nutritional state of the ruminant; (2) the lipolytic response of the AT to adrenergic stimulation is amplified by glucocorticoids and attenuated by growth hormone; (3) the AT of some sheep breeds is highly sensitive to the lipolytically potent catecholamines, which could be a key factor in their adaptation to undernutrition, especially in lactating ewes; (4

the amount and metabolism (lipolytic potential, leptin yield) of ruminant AT are related to body adiposity and to energy balance, and that these responses are amplified during lactations, and that the tail fat depot seems to be a key tissue in this respect.

the AT of underfed ruminant animals is characterized by: (1) a higher basal and stimulated lipolysis, (2) a lower lipogenic capacity, (3) a lower sensitivity to insulin, (4) a higher yield of leptin, (5) a higher sensitivity to glucocorticoids, (6) a higher sensitivity (or a lower resistance) to the lipogenic action of growth hormone.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the role of AT in adaptation to underfeeding and lactation, and in particular with the mechanisms of regulation of the AT metabolism, and of the interactions of AT with the endocrine and nervous systems.

the role of AT in the regulation of body energy stores and in the metabolic and endocrine responses to undernutrition.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
AT is an important organ of adaptation to undernutrition in lactating ruminants, especially in those breeds having a high fatness.
the AT of underfed animals is not a passive organ, but a highly plastic one which is able to adapt its metabolism and its endocrine function to the new nutritional status.

, in ruminant AT, the metabolic and endocrine responses to adrenergic stimulation are related to the animal’s nutritional status and body fatness, whereas the responses to insulin, glucocorticoids and leptin are related to the body fat set point.
The main takeaway from our work is that
AT plays an important role in ruminant adaptation to undernutrition, and that the AT responses to undernutrition are not the same in all species.
the AT metabolism in ruminants is highly flexible and that the metabolic adaptations of AT to undernutrition and lactation are complex and involve several endocrine factors.

the AT of ruminants is a dynamic and complex tissue, whose responses to underfeeding are not only related to body fat content, but also to the physiological and metabolic status of the animal, and to the type of underfeeding.
